title: Whether a provider url passed for one call may choose a private address, in three languages
pins: Whether a provider url passed for ONE call (`using(provider, model, {url})`) is refused before any request when it names a loopback, private, link-local, shared, unique-local, unspecified or cloud metadata address, written as a literal in the spellings an OS resolver reads (IPv6 forms that carry an IPv4 address included), or named by a stock hosts file, and whether a host is judged exactly as written: an escape, any character a hostname or address literal may not hold, or a format, invisible or IDNA deviation character, is refused rather than decoded or converted, and whether a non-ASCII host is refused with its own code (non_ascii_host_use_punycode) while its punycode form is sent. A per-call url is chosen by whoever builds the call, so a url that reaches 169.254.169.254 or a service behind the firewall in one language and is refused in another is an SSRF hole in whichever accepts it, and nothing errors to say so. Configured urls are the operator's and are deliberately not checked; they appear only as controls, together with the one explicit configuration opt-out and the proof that the call itself cannot turn it on.
scope: The openai provider and one named openai-compatible entry, entered through Prism.text().using() in each language. Address literals in decimal, octal, hex, shortened, IPv6, IPv4-mapped, NAT64, SIIT IPv4-translated and ISATAP spellings, the RHEL, openSUSE, Debian and macOS hosts-file names and names under localhost.localdomain, userinfo in front of the host, local and metadata names with case and trailing-dot variation, percent escapes in names, address literals and IPv6 literals, characters no host may hold, a backslash in the authority, zero-width joiners, other invisible characters and the IDNA deviation characters (U+1E9E included), non-ASCII hosts (an international name, names that fail the IDNA2008 bidi and hyphen rules, full-width digits) and the punycode forms of international names, IPv6 literals with a dotted IPv4 tail (public, and carrying a private address under ISATAP or NAT64), an empty written host, a public name with a trailing dot, one non-http scheme, and the configuration controls. Six per-call-wire rows (pcu-0094..pcu-0099) put userinfo in front of the host (a user name, a user name and password, a password alone, a percent-encoded @ inside the user name, an empty userinfo) plus a control without it, and run over each language's real default transport against a loopback server, with the per-call address check opted out in config so the endpoint is reachable. Twelve opt-out rows (pcu-0100..pcu-0111) turn the private-address opt-out on in config and give a per-call url another scheme (file, FILE, data, a <URL:...> wrapper, backslashes for slashes), a backslash before the at sign, a percent-escaped address or name, a non-ASCII host or full-width digits, once through a compatible entry's own opt-out, plus a control that is still sent. NOT covered: a public hostname that RESOLVES to a private address (no language resolves names here, by design: the check makes no network call), DNS rebinding, the reference's other providers and custom providers (each language's own regression tests cover those), and the refusal message, which is outside the contract.
construction: Native PHP manager entered through Prism::text()->using() with Laravel's HTTP fake and stray requests prevented, reading the package's own config/prism.php against each row's environment; native TypeScript Prism.text().using() with fetch captured; native Python Prism.text().using() with the default transport's send captured and DNS and sockets refused. Every fixture answers 500, because only whether a request went out matters. Each observation is `dispatched` and the refusal code, and nothing else: tools/per-call-url-guard/contract.mjs refuses any other field and any row both dispatched and refused. A per-call-wire row is the exception: tools/per-call-url-guard.mjs starts a raw TCP loopback server for it (tools/cross-origin-redirect/servers.mjs), fills its {endpoint}, and records `dispatched` as whether that server received a connection. PHP runs it over Laravel's real HTTP client with a global middleware refusing any non-127.x host, TypeScript over the real fetch wrapped to refuse any non-127.x host, and Python over the default transport with DNS and connections refused for anything but a 127.x literal. Those rows exist because every other row captures the request where the SDK hands it to its client, so a url the SDK builds but its platform client cannot send was recorded as sent.
findings: Corpus 0.1.40 adds twelve opt-out rows (G-382). The private-address opt-out used to switch off the whole per-call check in the reference and in TypeScript, so with it on a per-call url with another scheme or a host the check cannot read went to the provider unchecked; prism-py had already narrowed its opt-out to the address rules (prism-py#62). Against the code before the fix, each language fails all eleven hostile rows (PHP and TypeScript send them; prism-py before #62 sends them too) and the control is sent in all three. With the fix (prism `fix/g382-guard-judges-what-is-sent`, prism-ts `fix/g382-opt-out-keeps-shape-rules`, prism-py main) all twelve agree. A PHP "sent" before the fix is the built request as Laravel's fake captured it; its real client refuses a non-http scheme itself, but a custom provider or transport gets the url as given. Corpus 0.1.38 adds the six per-call-wire rows (G-382). Before them, no row in this suite or in credential-scope could see what a default transport does with a url carrying userinfo: both capture the built request, so credential-scope cs-0012, cs-0013 and cs-0026 record dispatched in all three languages, which is true of the request and says nothing about the client. Over the real clients, the rows do NOT agree, and that is recorded rather than aligned away: the reference sends a url with userinfo (Guzzle uses it as basic auth), and both ports refuse it with scheme_not_allowed before any connection, because neither platform client can send it (fetch refuses it; urllib read it as part of the host name). An empty userinfo (pcu-0099) is sent by PHP and TypeScript, whose parsers drop it, and refused by Python, which fails closed. Against prism-py main before the G-382 fix, the five userinfo rows record no refusal at all: the call failed only because the runner refused the name lookup it attempted for the userinfo. The control pcu-0094 is sent by all three. 93 of 93 rows agree on the fix branches (prism, prism-ts and prism-py `fix/g366-isatap-under-6to4`). Against the code before that fix, all three languages SENT the two ISATAP rows behind a 6to4 prefix, and refused the bracketed trailing dot only by accident of their URL parsers (PHP and Python accepted it), so 3 of the 4 new rows fail in every language. Before that, 89 of 89 agreed on `fix/g366-per-call-host-followups`. Against the code before that fix, the 12 rows added with it and the changed pcu-0055 fail 8 rows in PHP and 6 in each port: all three accepted U+1E9E inside localhost and in a public name and accepted the unicode international name; PHP refused the bidi-rule and hyphen-rule names with private_address_refused where the ports SENT them, and refused public IPv6 literals with a dotted IPv4 tail where the ports sent them. A non-ASCII per-call host is now refused with non_ascii_host_use_punycode in every language, before any conversion, and its punycode form is sent; no language runs IDNA on a per-call host any more. Before that, on the code before the G-365 fix, 77 of 77 rows ALSO agreed while 14 of the 22 rows added with it were SENT in all three languages, and on the code before the as-written host rule 43 of the first 55 agreed. The zero-width joiner rows, and the Persian name that needs one, record no refusal code in any language, because each language's clean-url check refuses them before the guard runs; the guard on its own refuses them too, which each language's unit rows assert, since this suite only enters through using(). Agreement here is a conclusion about behaviour, not about safety: the three guards follow one spec, so a shared misreading of it would agree here too. A hostname that resolves to a private address is not refused, in any language, because no language resolves names here.

discrimination.gap: No mutation probe is delivered for this suite. Four coarse negative controls: the code before the per-call guard fails 29 to 30 of the first 34 rows in every language; the code before the as-written host rule fails 12 of the first 55; the code before the G-365 fix sends 14 of the 22 rows added with it, in all three languages, while every row still agrees; and the code before the G-366 fix fails 8 rows in PHP and 6 in each port. The per-call-wire rows have one negative control: prism-py before the G-382 fix fails pcu-0095..pcu-0099. The opt-out rows have one negative control: the code before G-382 in each language fails pcu-0100..pcu-0109 and pcu-0111.

php.note: Run the corpus-loading entry point with php --check. PRISM_PHP_SRC points it at a prism checkout (CI uses the default branch); without it, it reads the installed reference in runners/php.

ts.note: Run the corpus-loading entry point with ts --check; it reads the built sibling prism-ts/dist, or PRISM_TS_DIST.

py.note: Run the corpus-loading entry point with py --check; it imports the installed package, or PRISM_PY_SRC.
